endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: AI is used in a manner which impacts access to care or impacts medical decision making at the point of care, that use of AI should be disclosed and documented to both physicians and/or patients in a culturally and linguistically appropriate manner.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing machine-assisted translation in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Ensure transparency regarding the use of AI in translating patient documents

endorsements.title: Achieving health equity through conversational AI: A roadmap for design and implementation of inclusive chatbots in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Enable multiple language translation for culturally and linguistically diverse communities

endorsements.title: Ethical Considerations in Personal Health Large Language Models
endorsements.quote: Inclusive design extends beyond outcome auditing: PH-LLMs should support languages prevalent in target populations, incorporate cultural adaptation beyond direct translation, conform to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.2 [ 129 ], and provide health-literacy adaptation through adjustable response complexity and optional comprehension checks [ 96 , 130 ].

endorsements.title: Personal Health Large Language Models and the Negotiation of Medical Authority in Clinical Care: Opportunities, Risks, and Governance
endorsements.quote: Health systems may reduce inequity through standardized previsit symptom forms, nonproprietary patient-reported outcome tools, interpreter-accessible digital supports, and staff-assisted intake, helping prevent PH-LLM use from becoming an informal gateway to more attentive care.

evidence.title: Assessment of Artificial Intelligence-based Translation Tools for Emergency Department Discharge Instructions
evidence.venue: The western journal of emergency medicine
evidence.outcome: Potentially harmful errors in AI translations of discharge instructions for LEP patients
evidence.effect: Microsoft Copilot and Google Translate produced a total of five potentially harmful translation errors; none were identified for ChatGPT-4.
evidence.quote: Both Microsoft Copilot and Google Translate produced a total of five potentially harmful translation errors, whereas none were identified for ChatGPT-4.
evidence.sample_unit: translated discharge instruction sets (4 topics x 3 languages x 3 tools)

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence Translation Tools for Language Equivalence of Oncology-Informed Consent Forms From English to Spanish
evidence.outcome: Language equivalence of AI-translated oncology consent forms versus certified Spanish translations, rated on 5-point scale
evidence.effect: Certified 4.99; ChatGPT-4o 4.89; DeepL Pro 4.43 (P<0.001 vs certified); Med_English2Spanish 3.32 (P<0.001). Variable equivalence; not suitable for clinical deployment without human review.
evidence.quote: While AI-generated translations are currently not suitable for clinical deployment without human review, this exploratory study supports further analysis of AI translation tools for reducing language barriers to LEP population enrollment.
evidence.sample_unit: oncology informed consent forms (each translated by 4 methods, scored by 2 physicians)

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether delivering AI-use disclosures in culturally and linguistically appropriate formats improves patient understanding or decisions. Five sources endorse the practice, and two offline studies suggest that machine translation of patient documents, one way a system might produce such disclosures, can introduce errors.

perspectives.view: No study in this set tests the practice. Support rests on one guidance document and four commentaries. The two available studies are offline, level 4 designs that examine the translation quality of discharge instructions and consent forms rather than the disclosure of AI use. They are indirect to the recommendation and cannot establish benefit.

In one offline study, Microsoft Copilot and Google Translate produced five potentially harmful errors in translated discharge instructions, and ChatGPT-4 produced none. In another, AI-translated Spanish consent forms scored 3.32 to 4.89 on equivalence, compared with 4.99 for certified translations. If disclosures are machine translated without review, the disclosure itself may carry errors.

The consent-form study rated three documents with two physician raters, and its authors judged AI translation unsuitable for clinical deployment without human review. This suggests that producing disclosures in many languages may require certified translators or bilingual reviewers. No study here has measured the staffing cost of that work.

Both hazard studies examined documents intended for patients with limited English proficiency, and one was set in a safety-net context. Neither measured whether patients understood AI-use disclosures. The studies show that translation quality varies by tool, but they do not address low-literacy formats, cultural adaptation beyond word-for-word translation, or the full range of languages patients speak.

Patients with limited English proficiency depend on translated text to learn that AI shaped their care. One endorsing commentary also calls for interpreter-accessible digital supports and staff-assisted intake, which would give patients a person to ask. No study reports how patients received or trusted a translated disclosure.

commentary.research_gap: No study has compared translated or culturally adapted AI-use disclosures with English-only or standard disclosures on patient comprehension, trust, or decision outcomes. Studies should test disclosure formats with limited English proficiency and low-literacy patients in real clinical settings. They should also measure translation error rates with and without human review and report the costs of each approach.
commentary.underserved_note: Neither study tested the practice. The two hazard studies addressed limited English proficiency populations, one in a safety-net setting and one with a racial and ethnic minority focus, but both were offline and examined document translation rather than disclosure. No study included low-literacy or Medicaid-specific samples, so effects for those groups remain unknown.
